title: 2 Kings 19:1–13
context: Hearing the Rabshakeh’s words, Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, goes into the LORD’s house, and sends his officials and the elders of the priests to Isaiah the son of Amoz, asking him to pray for the remnant that is left. Isaiah answers with the LORD’s word not to be afraid, for the LORD will put a spirit in the king of Assyria, cause him to hear news and return home, and fall by the sword in his own land. Hearing that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia has come out against him, the Assyrian king sends another message, this time warning Hezekiah not to let his God deceive him. A parallel account appears in Isaiah 37. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about humble dependence, prayer in crisis, and the LORD’s answer to those who defy the living God.

verses.text: When King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah tearing his clothes, wearing sackcloth, and going into the LORD’s house. In crisis he turns first to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his humility and repentance as the right response to danger and blasphemy. Both traditions commonly hold up the verse as a model of seeking God in distress.

verses.text: He sent Eliakim, who was over the household, Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah sending his officials and priests in sackcloth to Isaiah. He seeks the LORD’s word through the prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the delegation as honoring God’s appointed means of revelation. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as humble dependence on God’s word.

verses.text: They said to him, “Hezekiah says, ‘Today is a day of trouble, of rebuke, and of rejection; for the children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to deliver them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah describing a day of trouble, rebuke, and rejection, like a birth without strength to deliver. He admits complete helplessness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as an honest confession that only God can save. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the posture of faith that knows its own weakness.

verses.text: It may be the LORD your God will hear all the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of Assyria his master has sent to defy the living God, and will rebuke the words which the LORD your God has heard. Therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah hoping that the LORD will hear the Rabshakeh’s words and rebuke them, and asking Isaiah to pray for the remnant. Prayer is his strongest response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal to the living God as grounding hope in God’s honor. Readers in both traditions commonly read the request for intercession as a fitting act of faith.

verses.text: So the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah’s servants coming to Isaiah. The king’s urgent request is carried faithfully to the prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a simple step that brings the crisis before the LORD’s messenger. Both traditions commonly read it as a brief narrative transition.

verses.text: Isaiah said to them, “Tell your master this: ‘The LORD says, “Don’t be afraid of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Isaiah’s message telling Hezekiah not to be afraid of the blasphemous words. God answers fear with assurance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD taking the blasphemy as directed against himself. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as comfort for those who face mockery for their faith.

verses.text: Behold, I will put a spirit in him, and he will hear news, and will return to his own land. I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD promising to put a spirit in the Assyrian king, cause him to hear news, and make him fall by the sword in his own land. God will turn him back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign control over the enemy’s decisions and fate (compare Proverbs 21:1). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a promise fulfilled at the end of the chapter.

verses.text: So Rabshakeh returned and found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah; for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Rabshakeh returning to find his king fighting at Libnah. The Assyrian campaign continues elsewhere.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the movement as the first sign of the LORD’s word beginning to unfold. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the locations of Lachish and Libnah with appropriate caution.

verses.text: When he heard it said of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, “Behold, he has come out to fight against you,” he sent messengers again to Hezekiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Assyrian king hearing that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia has come out to fight. News begins to shift the situation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see this report as connected to the LORD’s promise that the king would hear news. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God working through events.

verses.text: “Tell Hezekiah king of Judah this: ‘Don’t let your God in whom you trust deceive you, saying, Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Assyrian king warning Hezekiah not to let his God deceive him. The attack on faith is renewed in writing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the charge that God deceives as the deepest blasphemy of all. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a direct challenge to the LORD’s faithfulness.

verses.text: Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, by destroying them utterly. Will you be delivered?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king pointing to Assyria’s destruction of all lands and asking whether Judah will be delivered. Past success breeds arrogance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boast as forgetting that Assyria’s power is under God’s rule (compare Isaiah 10:5). Both traditions commonly read the verse as pride resting on human achievement.

verses.text: Have the gods of the nations delivered them, which my fathers have destroyed—Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the children of Eden who were in Telassar?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king listing conquered peoples whose gods did not deliver them. He repeats his argument from history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as setting the LORD among idols, the same error as before. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the identification of these places with caution.

verses.text: Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, of Hena, and Ivvah?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king asking where the kings of conquered cities are now. Earthly power seems unstoppable to those who hear him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the taunt as preparing for the LORD to show that he is unlike any earthly king or god. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the end of the enemy’s case.
